chapters.heading: UNITED STATES CAPITOL POLICE REFORM AND ACCOUNTABILITY

sections.heading: Authority in House, Senate, and shared spaces
paragraphs: (a) In House-controlled areas, the Capitol Police shall act subject to the authority of the House of Representatives, the Speaker of the House, the Presiding Officer of the House, and the House Sergeant at Arms.

(b) In Senate-controlled areas, the Capitol Police shall act subject to the authority of the Senate, the President pro tempore of the Senate, the Presiding Officer of the Senate, and the Senate Sergeant at Arms.
(c) In shared congressional areas, the Capitol Police shall act under the direction of the Capitol Police Board and the Chief, consistent with this Act and any lawful regulation issued under it.

(d) The Capitol Police may act immediately in any House-controlled area, Senate-controlled area, or shared congressional area when necessary to protect life, prevent serious bodily injury, respond to violence, stop an active threat, prevent serious property damage, secure an emergency scene, or prevent an immediate obstruction of congressional business.

(e) A lawful direction from the Speaker, President pro tempore, Presiding Officer, or relevant Sergeant at Arms concerning access, order, decorum, safety, removal of disorderly persons, or security within that House’s controlled spaces shall control within those spaces, except when immediate action is necessary to protect life, prevent serious bodily injury, or respond to an active emergency.

(f) The Capitol Police may assist the Sergeant at Arms of either House in preserving order, enforcing access rules, removing disorderly persons, escorting witnesses, securing committee rooms, protecting Members and officers, responding to threats, and carrying out lawful orders relating to the security of that House.

(g) The Capitol Police shall not remove a Member of Congress from the floor of either House, prevent a Member from entering the chamber of that Member’s House, prevent a Member from voting, prevent a Member from speaking when recognized, or otherwise interfere with a legislative proceeding unless acting pursuant to the rules of the relevant House or responding to an immediate threat of violence or serious danger.

(h) The Capitol Police may deny entry to, remove, or detain any person who is not a Member of Congress when such person is unlawfully present, refuses to comply with lawful access rules, disrupts congressional business, threatens the safety of another person, obstructs an entrance or proceeding, or violates a lawful order issued by the relevant House, Presiding Officer, Sergeant at Arms, Board, Chief, or officer acting under lawful authority.

(i) Where a security action directly affects a chamber proceeding, committee proceeding, Member of Congress, officer of Congress, witness, or invited guest, the Chief shall ensure that the relevant Sergeant at Arms is notified as soon as practicable.

(j) In any conflict between an ordinary operational order of the Chief and a lawful order of the relevant House, Speaker, President pro tempore, Presiding Officer, or Sergeant at Arms concerning that House’s controlled spaces or proceedings, the order of the relevant House authority shall control unless immediate emergency action is required.

(k) The Chief shall maintain procedures for coordination between Capitol Police officers and the Sergeants at Arms of both Houses so that officers assigned to chamber entrances, galleries, committee rooms, hearings, and secured proceedings understand the rules, access requirements, and chain of authority applicable to those spaces.

sections.heading: Protection of Members, officers, employees, witnesses, and guests
paragraphs: (a) The Capitol Police may provide protective services for Members of Congress, officers of Congress, congressional employees, witnesses, invited guests, visitors, and other persons whose safety is connected to the conduct of official congressional business.

(b) Protective services may be provided where a person is present within the United States Capitol Buildings and Grounds, attending or participating in a congressional proceeding, traveling for official congressional business, appearing before either House or a committee, assisting a congressional investigation, or otherwise exposed to a threat because of duties, testimony, employment, invitation, or association with Congress.

(c) Protective services may include physical security, escorts, secure transportation, access control, threat assessment, site security, emergency response, coordination with other lawful security agencies, and any other measure reasonably necessary to protect the person, preserve order, or prevent interference with official congressional business.

(d) The Board may authorize continuing protective services for a Member of Congress, officer of Congress, witness, congressional employee, or other person where threats, official duties, public exposure, travel, leadership responsibilities, committee activity, investigative work, or other security concerns make such protection necessary.

(e) The Chief may authorize temporary protective services without prior approval of the Board where an immediate threat exists, where delay would endanger the person to be protected, or where protection is necessary to secure an ongoing congressional proceeding, hearing, meeting, inspection, ceremony, or official function.

(f) Temporary protective services authorized by the Chief shall be limited to the time and measures reasonably necessary to address the threat, official function, travel, emergency, or security concern that justified the protection.

(g) The Chief shall report any temporary protective service involving an immediate threat, outside law enforcement assistance, travel outside the United States Capitol Buildings and Grounds, use of force, detention, arrest, evacuation, or substantial expenditure of personnel or resources to the Board as soon as practicable.

(h) The Capitol Police may protect a witness or invited guest before, during, and after a congressional proceeding where the person’s safety, access, testimony, cooperation, or ability to participate in congressional business may be threatened, obstructed, intimidated, or disrupted.

(i) The Capitol Police may protect congressional employees and staff where threats or safety concerns arise from their official duties, employment in a congressional office, service to a committee, handling of sensitive information, public-facing responsibilities, or presence at a congressional proceeding or secured area.

(j) Protective services shall not be used to shield any person from lawful process, prevent congressional oversight, avoid questioning by either House or a committee, obstruct an investigation, interfere with a lawful arrest, or prevent the execution of any lawful order issued by Congress, either House, a committee, a court, or another lawful authority.

(k) The Chief shall maintain records of protective services provided under this section, including the person or category of person protected, the general basis for protection, the duration of protection, the type of protection provided, any outside agency involved, and any security incident connected to the protection.

(l) Records concerning protective services may be maintained in closed form where disclosure would endanger a protected person, reveal sensitive security procedures, compromise an active threat response, or expose private personal information, but such records shall remain available for lawful review by the Board.
